name: John Dewey
role: American philosopher, psychologist and educational reformer (1859–1952)
summary: Dewey was a pragmatist who treated democracy as a way of shared living and joint inquiry rather than only a form of government, and distrusted rule by experts or elites. From the 1930s he rejected laissez-faire liberalism and argued for a socialized, planned economy reached by democratic means, supported unions, workers' rights and a welfare state, and opposed both fascism and Soviet communism. He criticized national-sovereignty absolutism, backed the outlawry of war and an international order, and held that policies and institutions should be judged by tested consequences rather than by general doctrines.

notes: Mature position: the 1927-1935 books (The Public and Its Problems, Individualism Old and New, Liberalism and Social Action); German Philosophy and Politics (1915) and Democracy and Education (1916) are earlier but consistent. Dewey supported US entry into the First World War (SEP) and later regretted the optimism behind it; no statement here rests on that. Positions the SEP states are medium confidence. Themes searched in the local Gutenberg corpus and archive.org texts: economy and property, planning, unions, democracy and experts, the state, force and revolution, war and internationalism, China and Japan, education, character and habit. Little found on guns, policing, immigration, abortion, religion in public life, environment or technology policy. Freedom and Culture (1939), Why I Am Not a Communist (1934) and Dewey's 1923 outlawry of war essays were not available in open full text.
